Side-Lin
items.body: Die Krupps, the German industrial and EBM band from Düsseldorf, released “V – Metal Machine Music” on 28 August 2015 through Oblivion and Steamhammer, with distribution by SPV. The album turns 11 this year. Metropolis Records handled the North American edition. It was the ninth Die Krupps studio album and the follow-up to “The Machinists of Joy” from 2013, and it appeared as a double CD in a six-panel digipak, as a digital download and as a limited box set. Side-Line’s own pre-order item of 5 August 2015, Die Krupps announce ‘V: Metal Machine’ 2CD album for September – pre-orders accepted now!, put the release in September. Wikipedia, Discogs and MusicBrainz all give 28 August 2015 for the German edition, and that is the date used here. The title reaches back into the band’s own catalogue. “Metal Machine Music” was a 1992 single from the album “I”, named in turn after Lou Reed’s 1975 record, which Jürgen Engler has credited as an influence on the band. Engler and Marcel Zürcher wrote the music except where noted, with lyrics split between Engler and Ralf Dörper. Engler and Chris Lietz produced the record, Alex Henke recorded additional guitar and Sascha Osterland made the artwork. Disc one runs thirteen tracks: “Die Verdammten (Prelude)”, “Kaltes Herz”, “Battle Extreme”, “Fly Martyrs Fly”, “The Truth”, “Road Rage Warrior”, “The Vampire Strikes Back”, “Alive in a Glass Cage”, “Branded”, “Kaos Reigns”, “The Red Line”, “Bonded by Blood” and “Volle Kraft Voraus”. Several of those are older pieces revisited. The prelude reworks the intro tape the band used on its 2011 and 2014 tours and takes its music from Maurice Jarre. “The Vampire Strikes Back” first surfaced on a Wing Commander soundtrack in 1998, the last song the band recorded before its 1997 break. “Alive in a Glass Cage”, “Road Rage Warrior” and “Volle Kraft Voraus” are re-recordings, the last of them the title track of the 1982 album. “The Red Line” had already appeared in a different version as the B-side to the 2014 single “Robo Sapien”. Side-Line reviewed the album on 10 October 2015 and placed it next to the band’s 1990s run of “I”, “II – The Final Option”, “III – Odyssey Of The Mind” and “Paradise Now”, with the guitars sitting further forward. The review stated: “Mastermind Jurgen Engler, currently living in Austin-Texas (USA), still can’t choose between pure electronic music and guitars and succeeds in combining both in a powerful way!” The full text is in Die Krupps – V – Metal Machine Music (DCD Album – SPV/Steamhammer/Oblivion Records). Die Krupps’ ‘V – Metal Machine Music’ singles and bonus disc “Battle Extreme” / “Fly Martyrs Fly” arrived two weeks ahead of the album, on 14 August 2015, with a lyric video for the A-side that Side-Line covered in New Die Krupps video hits the net: ‘Battle Extreme’. “Kaltes Herz” followed on 16 October 2015 with “Branded” as its B-side and a promo video directed by Faderhead. “Alive in a Glass Cage” came out on 28 July 2016, re-recorded with Caliban and issued before the band’s first Wacken Open Air appearance. The second disc carries eight tracks: a Darkhaus rework of “Kaltes Herz”, a Faderhead remix of “Alive in a Glass Cage”, “Road Rage Warrior ’82” and demo versions of “Battle Extreme”, “Kaos Reigns”, “The Vampire Strikes Back”, “Kaltes Herz” and “Alive in a Glass Cage”. Dependent Records reissued both the standard and the deluxe running order digitally in 2025. About Die Krupps Jürgen Engler, Ralf Dörper and Bernward Malaka formed Die Krupps in Düsseldorf in 1980. The name comes from the Krupp industrial dynasty, and the band has pointed to Luchino Visconti’s 1969 film “The Damned” as the starting point. The debut album “Stahlwerksynfonie” appeared in 1981 and set factory noise and metallic percussion against conventional instruments. The EP “Wahre Arbeit, wahrer Lohn” followed the same year. Dörper left in 1982 to form Propaganda. “Volle Kraft voraus!” arrived in 1982 and moved toward synthesizers while keeping the metal percussion. “Entering the Arena” in 1985 dropped most of that percussion and carried the band’s first English-language material. Engler then ran the Atom-H label, signing thrash metal and hardcore punk acts, and that catalogue fed back into the band’s next decade. In 1989 Dörper started a collaboration with Nitzer Ebb on “Machineries of Joy”, a new version of the early track “Wahre Arbeit, wahrer Lohn”, which he produced with Engler. Its chart placing led to the band restarting with Engler and Dörper at the front. Guitars entered the sound in 1992 with the album “I” and the Metallica covers EP “A Tribute to Metallica”. “II – The Final Option” followed in 1993, “III – Odyssey of the Mind” in 1995 and “Paradise Now” in 1997, after which the band stopped. Engler started DKay.com the same year and released “Decaydenz” in 2000 and “Deeper into the Heart of Dysfunction” in 2002. Die Krupps returned to the stage for their 25th anniversary across 2005 and 2006, and the two “Too Much History” compilations appeared in autumn 2007. The remix album “Volle Kraft Null Acht” came in 2009 and the EP “Als wären wir für immer” in 2010, the first new material since 1997. A joint European tour with Nitzer Ebb followed in 2011. “The Machinists of Joy” arrived in 2013 as the first full album in sixteen years, and “V – Metal Machine Music” came two years later. The band re-recorded its debut as “Stahlwerkrequiem” in 2016, reported in Die Krupps re-records 1981 debut album ‘Stahlwerksinfonie’ for vinyl (incl. CD) release, and the live set “Live im Schatten der Ringe”, taped in 2014, followed on DVD, Blu-ray and 2CD, covered in Watch trailer new Die Krupps live DVD & Blu-ray (incl. 2CD) ‘Live Im Schatten Der Ringe’ – out this Friday. Engler launched the EBM side project Die Robo Sapiens in February 2018, announced in Die Krupps frontman Jürgen Engler launches EBM-only project Die Robo Sapiens, and its debut album “Robo Sapien Race” arrived in October 2022. The same spring the band announced a single and a tour with Front Line Assembly. “Vision 2020 Vision” was announced for November 2019 in Die Krupps return with a new album in November: ‘Vision 2020 Vision’, and Engler formed the industrial metal group Die Klute that year with Dino Cazares of Fear Factory and Claus Larsen of Leæther Strip. The covers album Songs from the Dark Side of Heaven came in March 2021, and the band’s first live recording, from 1981, was issued as The Big Industrial Bang on CD and DVD in April of the same year. Marcel Zürcher, guitarist since 2005, left in 2023, and Nils Finkeisen covered guitar until 2024. The line-up is now Engler on vocals, guitars and keyboards, Dörper on keyboards, synthesizers and programming, Paul Keller on drums and Dylan Smith on guitars. In August 2025 the band signed a multi-album deal with Dependent Records, reported in Die Krupps sign multi-album deal with Dependent Records; new album due in 2026, and followed it with the tour-only EP Will nicht – MUSS! / On Collision Course. Engler and Dörper looked back across the run in Ralf Dörper interview on why Die Krupps still won’t behave and Die Krupps interview on the 45 Years of Industrial Steel North America Tour. Eleven years on, “V – Metal Machine Music” sits between “The Machinists of Joy” and “Vision 2020 Vision” in that sequence.

items.body: German electronic composer Michael Brückner released “The Egg in the Cosmic Crack” through the Argentine label Cyclical Dreams on 28 August 2026. The album runs six tracks and 77 minutes of Berlin School sequencing and ambient, and is out on digital platforms, as a download and on CD. Two of those tracks are almost twenty years old. The opener “The Egg of Ecquirlo” began as a giveaway Brückner made in 2007 for members of a Last.fm group he had founded, a track he kept meaning to place on a proper album. “Cracked Egg Mystification” came out of the same set of preoccupations and went to the Cerebral Audio compilation “The Rift: Volume 1” in 2016. Both were remixed, partly rearranged, remastered and given new detail for this release. From unused material left over from the 2007 sessions, plus fresh parts, Brückner assembled “The Egg of Ecquirlo – Part 2”, then recorded further pieces to complete the record. The thread running through all of it is a book. Brückner started making music at 21, prompted by meditative yoga practice, and through those studies read Joseph Chilton Pearce’s “The Crack in the Cosmic Egg”. Cyclical Dreams describes the result as “music based on the idea of the egg as a universal symbol”, and the album notes report that those early influences still inform Brückner’s music decades on. There is wordplay underneath the concept. The word “eye” appears in two of the titles, “Joseph’s Eye” and “The Eye of Cyclops”, and sounds like the German “Ei”, meaning egg. Brückner built the album on a wide spread of hardware and software instruments: the Waldorf Blofeld, Behringer DeepMind 6 and Model D, Moog Labyrinth, Korg Z1, NI Absynth, Cherry Audio Rhodes Chroma, GX-80 and Elka-X, u-he Hive 2 and the Moog Theremini. Cyclical Dreams handled the artwork, with photography by Amp Puttipong. The Egg in the Cosmic Crack by Michael Brückner Michael Brückner’s six tracks and where to hear them “The Egg of Ecquirlo – Part 1” (22:23) “Coda (A Pure Oval Shape)” (4:54) “Joseph’s Eye” (13:28) “Cracked Egg Mystification (Revisited)” (13:52) “The Egg of Ecquirlo – Part 2” (10:08) “The Eye of Cyclops” (12:49) The album is on Bandcamp and across digital platforms, with a download edition through Payhip and a CD pressed on demand through the label’s Kunaki storefront. Cyclical Dreams has also put the full album on YouTube. About Michael Brückner Michael Brückner was born in Heidelberg in 1969 and settled near Mainz, where he works as a graphic designer. He began composing and recording electronic music in 1992 without formal training, after the experience of mantra chanting in a yoga group, and started circulating his work through online networks from 2006. His output has run to well over a hundred albums, most of them downloads and CDrs, and he has performed live at smaller festivals and solo since 2012. His music sits mainly in ambient and Berlin School, with long sequenced passages and drifting synth layers. He records with several groups alongside his solo work, including P’Faun, Bridge To Imla and La Mansarde Hérmetique, and has collaborated with Mathias Grassow, Volker Lankow and Mathias Brüssel among others. Brückner has released steadily through Cyclical Dreams, the Buenos Aires label whose catalogue covers Berlin School, ambient, soundscape, space music and drone. His albums for it include “Footprints”, “Recycled Life”, “Twenty-Five Light Years”, “The Morphic Cycle”, “The Seven Planes of Dreams” in 2024 and “A Sequence of Colours” in December 2025. Side-Line has followed the label’s recent output, including D*Time’s “Nightwoven” and Christian Wittman‘s “Andromeda”. “The Egg in the Cosmic Crack” reaches further back than any of them, finishing a piece of music Brückner has carried since 2007.

items.body: Buzz Kull released a video for “In the Cut” on 26 August 2026, two weeks before the Sydney project starts a North American tour with Kontravoid. The track comes from “Deep Hate”, the EP Marc Dwyer issued through Heartworm Press on 13 February 2026. Chris Fatseas directed the video, which puts Dwyer opposite Sydney model Andrea. Buzz Kull’s ‘Deep Hate’ EP and its remix edition “Deep Hate” holds four tracks: “Black Gate”, “In The Cut”, “Just A Memory” and “Human Force”. Dwyer wrote and recorded all four, Ewan Kay mixed and mastered them, and Jonathan Schenke added mixing on “In The Cut”. Wes Eisold of Cold Cave sings on “Human Force”, which also carries an additional drum mix by Alex Garcia-Rivera. Amy Lee handled design and Shaun Daniel the photography. Heartworm Press pressed the EP as a 12-inch at 45 RPM in a black-and-white split variant and in a red-and-black marble “Bloodlust” edition limited to 100 copies. The CD and digital editions add four remixes: “Black Gate” reworked by PIG, “In The Cut” by Kontravoid, “Just A Memory” by Cold Cave and “Human Force” by Spike Hellis. Buzz Kull and Kontravoid tour dates The co-headline run opens on 10 September at Elysium in Austin as part of Levitation and closes on 24 October at Below at The Belasco in Los Angeles. Normal Bias supports the Brooklyn show, and Spike Hellis and Normal Bias join the Spokane, Vancouver, Seattle, Portland and Sacramento dates. 10 September 2026 – Austin, TX, US – Elysium (Levitation) 11 September 2026 – Houston, TX, US – Barbarella 12 September 2026 – New Orleans, LA, US – Santos Bar 13 September 2026 – Atlanta, GA, US – The EARL 15 September 2026 – Tampa, FL, US – The Orpheum 16 September 2026 – Orlando, FL, US – Will’s Pub 18 September 2026 – Baltimore, MD, US – Metro Baltimore 19 September 2026 – Philadelphia, PA, US – Nikki Lopez 20 September 2026 – Brooklyn, NY, US – Saint Vitus 22 September 2026 – Montreal, QC, Canada – Foufounes Electriques 24 September 2026 – Toronto, ON, Canada – Cafeteria 25 September 2026 – Millvale, PA, US – The Funhouse at Mr. Smalls 26 September 2026 – Milwaukee, WI, US – Anodyne Coffee Roasting Co. 28 September 2026 – Minneapolis, MN, US – Icehouse 1 October 2026 – Indianapolis, IN, US – The 808 at Indy CD & Vinyl 2 October 2026 – Kansas City, MO, US – Encore at Uptown 3 October 2026 – Denver, CO, US – HQ 4 October 2026 – Salt Lake City, UT, US – Metro Music Hall 6 October 2026 – Spokane, WA, US – The Big Dipper 8 October 2026 – Vancouver, BC, Canada – Biltmore Cabaret 9 October 2026 – Seattle, WA, US – El Corazon 10 October 2026 – Portland, OR, US – Star Theater 13 October 2026 – Reno, NV, US – The Holland Project 15 October 2026 – Sacramento, CA, US – The Starlet Room 16 October 2026 – Las Vegas, NV, US – Backstage Bar & Billiards 23 October 2026 – San Francisco, CA, US – Great American Music Hall (Substance) 24 October 2026 – Los Angeles, CA, US – Below at The Belasco (Substance) Side-Line published the tour announcement in Buzz Kull and Kontravoid announce 2026 North American tour. About Buzz Kull Buzz Kull is the solo project of Sydney musician Marc Dwyer, active since 2012. He mixes darkwave, EBM and minimal synth, and has worked with Rebecca Liston in the live line-up. The project’s first singles, “I Disappear” and “Dreams”, appeared through Fabrika Records in 2013 and 2014. The debut album “Chroma” followed in 2017 and “New Kind of Cross” in 2018, with a run of singles including “Nausea”, “Avoiding The Light”, “Last In The Club”, “Rise From Yur Grave” and “Dancing With Machines” issued through Avant! Records between 2017 and 2022. Side-Line covered the return in Australia’s dark electro act Buzz Kull returns with all new album, the first new work since 2019, which announced the third album “Fascination” on Avant! Records in 2022. Dwyer moved to Eskimo Recordings for the 2023 single “A Place That’s Meant To Be”, then to Cleopatra Records for four singles across 2024 and 2025. “Just A Memory” opened his run on Heartworm Press in 2025 and led into “Deep Hate”, his first release for the label, in February 2026. The “In the Cut” video is the project’s latest, arriving as the North American dates begin.

items.body: Boy Harsher released a lyric video for “Tough Luck (When You Don’t Call)” on 26 August 2026, the third advance single from “Get Mean”, out 18 September 2026 on Atlantic Records. The Northampton duo of Jae Matthews and Augustus Muller follow “Jeans” and “Hard Beat” with a track built around a repeated “I’m OK” and the line “Do you even know my name?”. Los Angeles video artist Sean McGuirk assembled the clip on vintage video gear, styling it as an analog karaoke screen: a CRT television, cold blue background, thick yellow capitals and visible scan lines, with cards reading “IN THE STYLE OF” and “INSTRUMENTAL BREAK”. Jesse Korman shot the footage at PropHaus Brooklyn. What Boy Harsher put on ‘Get Mean’ The album runs twelve tracks: “Ronny”, “Jeans”, “Break Me”, “Tough Luck (When You Don’t Call)”, “Faulty”, “Coming Home”, “Hard Beat”, “Ice Pick (Walk Away)”, “Ivy’s Spiral”, “Pray 4 Me”, “Falling” and “Bleed”. Matthews and Muller recorded it across eight locations in the United States, Mexico and Italy, after Matthews wrote much of the material travelling through West Texas, the Pacific Northwest and South Florida. The pair ended their romantic relationship in early 2024 and the writing period also took in family loss. Matthews has kept her description of the record short. She calls it “what I had to give during the most extreme period of my life.” The sound picks up detuned pads, abrasive synth leads, pedal-steel bends, new wave guitar and unprocessed phone recordings. It is the duo’s first album since the 2022 short film and soundtrack “The Runner”. Atlantic issues “Get Mean” on 140g black vinyl with a 12 x 24 inch poster, on an indie-exclusive blue marble pressing, on a Record Store Day blue variant and on CD. Pre-orders run through Bandcamp via Nude Club Records, the duo’s own imprint, and through record shops. Side-Line covered the signing and the album announcement in Boy Harsher signs to Atlantic Records, announces ‘Get Mean’. The Heartbreak Tour reaches North America from 25 September and Europe and the UK from 14 November, closing in Antwerp on 4 December. Dates in Denver, Paris, Glasgow and Bristol have now sold out, joining the Chicago, Portland, Seattle, Vancouver and Los Angeles shows already gone. The full itinerary is listed in Boy Harsher announce ‘The Heartbreak Tour’ North American dates for 2026. Matthews and Muller have also directed and scored a feature-length horror thriller, “The Lonely Woman”, with a cast including Chloë Sevigny, FKA twigs, Sturgill Simpson, Will Oldham and Jake Weary. About Boy Harsher Jae Matthews and Augustus Muller met at film school in Savannah, Georgia, and began working together in 2013 as Teen Dreamz, with Matthews performing spoken word over Muller’s backing. They took the name Boy Harsher in January 2014 and issued the home-recorded “Lesser Man” EP as a cassette. DKA Records released their first album, “Yr Body Is Nothing”, in 2016, followed by the “Country Girl” EP in 2017 and singles including “Motion”, “Run” and “Face the Fire”. The pair founded their own label, Nude Club, in 2018 and reissued the back catalogue through it. “Pain II” arrived that year with a remix by The Soft Moon. The album “Careful” followed in 2019, with “Country Girl Uncut” and a remix set the same year. Side-Line rated “Careful” 8½ on release. The duo relocated to Northampton, Massachusetts. In January 2022 they released “The Runner”, a short film starring Kristina Esfandiari that streamed on Shudder, together with its soundtrack and the “Burn It Down” EP. Festival appearances between 2022 and 2024 included Primavera Sound, Roadburn, Cruel World and Coachella, and in November 2024 they featured on the Pet Shop Boys double A-side “New London Boy / All The Young Dudes”. Muller also runs Safe Mind with Cooper B. Handy, whose album “Cutting the Stone” appeared on 25 July 2025. Boy Harsher signed to Atlantic Records in July 2026. “Get Mean” is their first album for the label and their first full-length in four years.

items.body: Bradford post-punk band 1919 release the two-track single “Last Dance of the Departed” on 13 November 2026, backed with “Satellite Man”. It is the group’s first 7-inch since the “Cry Wolf” single of 1983 and their first studio release since 2021. Pre-orders run through Bandcamp in four formats: a black 7-inch, a limited green 7-inch pressed in an edition of 300, a CD single, and a digital download at 24-bit/96kHz. Physical copies ship on or around the release date. The single carries a Cry Wolf/Engineer Records credit. 1919 line-up and recording credits Simon “Ding” Archer recorded both tracks at 6db Studios in Salford. He plays bass and handles programming in the current line-up, alongside Rio Goldhammer on vocals, Sam Evans on guitar and founding drummer Mick Reed. Goldhammer wrote the lyrics and produced the sleeve design. Goldhammer also directed the video for “Last Dance of the Departed”, posted to the band’s YouTube channel on 21 August 2026. It cuts together live and archive footage contributed by more than a dozen photographers, DJs and promoters, each credited by name. The B-side title is not new to the catalogue. 1919 self-released a digital EP called “Satellite Man” on 24 December 2021, which was until now their most recent studio material. About 1919 1919 formed in Bradford, England, in 1980 around guitarist Mark Tighe and vocalist Ian Tilleard, who had started out as Heaven Seventeen before taking the name 1919 from a book in Tighe’s collection. Bassist Nick Hiles and drummer Mick Reed completed the first settled line-up. Reed described the intent as “to create a heavy melodic intense dance band with no frills and no intentions”. The band issued “Repulsion” / “Tear Down These Walls” as a white-label 7-inch promo in 1982, then re-released it through Red Rhino Records, which also carried the “Caged” single and the mini-album “Machine” in March 1983. They recorded a first John Peel session in May 1982 and a second on 4 May 1983. Steve Madden replaced Hiles that year. Abstract Records issued the “Cry Wolf” 7-inch and 12-inch in 1983 and the “Earth Song” 12-inch in July 1984, after the group had already split. Kev Aston on saxophone and Paul “Sputnik” Drake on synthesizer appeared with the band at various points. Members went on to 1919 AD, The Hive and Another Cinema, all of which had ended by 1986. Tighe restarted the band in 2014 with bassist and vocalist Rio Goldhammer, self-releasing the download “Revenge” in 2015. Reed returned on drums on 30 August 2015 and Karl Donner joined on bass, moving Goldhammer to vocals. Westworld Recordings released the album “Bloodline” on 3 March 2017. Tighe died on 28 January 2017 at the age of 56, after a cancer diagnosis the previous year, and the band published an obituary in four languages; Side-Line reported it in British post-punk legends 1919 announce death guitar player Mark Tighe. Sam Evans joined as full-time guitarist in April 2017. Steve Madden died shortly before “Futurecide” appeared on Cleopatra Records on 12 April 2019; the album carries Tighe’s last recorded performance, on “Stop the World”, and Madden’s, on “Isolation”. Side-Line ran the first play of that album and its video in Side-Line exclusive: UK post-punk band 1919 premieres new video and album!. Archer, previously a bassist and producer with The Fall, PJ Harvey and Red Lorry Yellow Lorry, replaced Donner on 31 August 2020. The Paris label Manic Depression released the album “Citizens of Nowhere” on 25 June 2021, and the self-released “Satellite Man” EP followed that December. The band made their US debut in Los Angeles in 2023 after a Wave-Gotik-Treffen appearance in Leipzig. “Last Dance of the Departed” is their first new studio recording since 2021.

items.body: Reinhard Hüber brought T.A.N.K. to life in 2001 as a solo project, later joined by additional members for live performances. After more than 20 years, this is only the third album from the German EBM project. Several years have elapsed between releases, making each album feel somewhat like a new beginning, although I don’t think the EBM audience ever truly forgot T.A.N.K. “Broken Mirror” is the first album in nine years and also the project’s first release on Electro Aggression Records. It features 13 tracks plus five remixes and even a cover version. T.A.N.K. stands for vintage EBM—tracks that drive straight ahead. Typical heavy EBM basslines are paired with dark string arrangements, all set to a danceable rhythm. Here and there, a brief respite appears in the form of a slower tempo, where the EBM takes on a more atmospheric quality. Perhaps slightly atypical is Hüber’s harder, deep, distorted vocal style. While this is more common in Dark Electro productions, it works perfectly here. Among the tracks, I have a particular soft spot for “Zombie March” and its hilarious lyrics. After all, EBM rarely features profound lyrics—and that’s not something I personally expect from the genre anyway! Remixes were provided by Pyrroline, Sleepwalk, Serpents, Synaptic Defect, and Trilogy. The intelligent remix by Pyrroline, in particular, is an absolute treat for the ears. Finally, we get a somewhat surprising cover of R010R’s “Bloodsucker,” recast in a dark EBM mould. T.A.N.K. strikes back again with a solid, old-school EBM record that has been well crafted. Perhaps it could have been a bit harder overall for my taste, but otherwise, I have no complaints. (Rating:7½). Side-Line reported the announcement in April 2026, when Electro Aggression Records set “Broken Mirror” for release on May 30. Listen to “Zombie March”: Zombie March by T.A.N.K. About T.A.N.K. Reinhard Hüber, who came out of the 1990s German punk scene, launched T.A.N.K. in Dessau in 2001. The name stands for “Taktischer Angriff (auf’s) Nervenkostüm”. The first live appearance took place at the first Electric Tremor Festival in Dessau on 22 March 2002. The self-released “T.A.N.K.” EP landed in 2002, followed by the debut album “Musica Denaturale” on Ars Electrique in 2003. In 2011 the project contributed “Game of Men” to the 4CD set “Old School Electrology Volume One”. The second full-length, “Return”, came out in 2017 on Electric Tremor Dessau. Hüber also turned up in the Electro Aggression Records orbit through remix work connected to R010R and Synaptic Defect. “Broken Mirror” is the project’s third album and holds 19 tracks.

items.body: Vampire Valentine, the darkwave and post-punk duo from Newcastle upon Tyne, release their self-titled debut album “Vampire Valentine” on Morella Records on 28 August 2026. The record runs to 16 tracks and 78 minutes, and comes out on digital platforms and on CD. The album closes a year that began with a signature. Vampire Valentine signed to Morella Records on 15 January 2026 as the label’s first act, a date Morella now marks as its own founding anniversary. Michael Longstaff handles vocals and co-production, Kieron Wright plays bass and guitar, and US producer Ricky Conover supplies the synth and instrumental work that runs between the songs. Tony Gunk and label founder Blake Carpenter also produced, with Carpenter contributing guitar and handling mixing and mastering. The duo bring angular guitars, driving bass and vocals pitched between melody and unease, mixing post-punk urgency with gothic atmosphere, cyberpunk ambience and 1980s synth work. Five singles ran ahead of the album across 2026: “Tears” on 14 February and “Skin” on 27 March, then three drawn from the album itself, “In The Dark” on 19 June, “Cutting Ties” on 24 July and “Another Day” on 7 August. Longstaff describes the record as an unedited version of the band rather than a polished one. “We didn’t set out to make something comfortable. Every song on this record came from somewhere real, and we weren’t interested in softening any of it. This is us, completely, for the first time at full length.” Carpenter explains why the album was worth building the label around. “Vampire Valentine were the first artists to sign to Morella Records, and this album is exactly why. There was no hedging in what they were, not from the very first conversation. You can hear it in this record: The Cure, Bauhaus, all of it filtered through a band that already knew exactly who they are, finally given the room to say all of it at once.” VAMPIRE VALENTINE by Vampire Valentine Vampire Valentine’s debut album: the 16 tracks “Suffocation” “In The Dark” “Cutting Ties” “August Heat” “Imperfect” “The Other Side” “Empty Heart Heavy Eyes” “You Weren’t There For Me” “Obelisk” “Another Day” “Resurrect” “Don’t Talk About It” “Forsaken” “Black Sky” “Final Breath” “Lovesong (The Cure Cover)” Six of the sixteen tracks are instrumentals, most of them Conover’s. “August Heat”, “The Other Side”, “Obelisk”, “Forsaken”, “Black Sky” and “Final Breath” break up the vocal songs, with “The Other Side” reworking the chord progression of “Imperfect” at a faster tempo and “Final Breath” closing the record on ambient synth. Longstaff has said the closer brings survival horror games such as Resident Evil and Silent Hill to mind. Among the vocal tracks, “Resurrect” is the band’s tribute to Bauhaus, built around the idea of being undead, and takes Longstaff’s delivery to its harshest point on the record. “You Weren’t There For Me” is the song he has called the one he is most personally tied to, though he has not said who it is about. The Cure cover “Lovesong” closes the running order and is exclusive to the Bandcamp edition. The album is available on all digital platforms and as a deluxe CD shipping from the UK through the Morella Records store and the band’s Bandcamp page. About Vampire Valentine Vampire Valentine formed in October 2025 in Newcastle upon Tyne, founded by singer and producer Michael Longstaff and bassist and guitarist Kieron Wright. The duo cite The Sisters of Mercy and Twin Tribes among their reference points, and mix gothic rock, post-punk and darkwave with synth work from US producer Ricky Conover, who records as Forerunnerx. Their first releases came out on their own Bandcamp page: the single “Porcelain” on 14 November 2025, followed by an instrumental edition, and “Thorns” on 1 December 2025. On 15 January 2026 they signed to Morella Records, the independent label founded that same month by Blake Carpenter and based in Georgia in the United States, with a roster covering goth rock, deathrock, darkwave and post-punk. Vampire Valentine were the label’s first signing. The year that followed produced the album “Dry Remains” on 14 January 2026, the “Pale Dawn” EP on 17 April, and the five singles that led into the debut. Side-Line covered the run as it went out, from “In The Dark” through the “Cutting Ties” single to the album announcement in June, when the release still carried no exact date. The self-titled album gathers that year into one 78-minute record and is the duo’s first full-length under the Morella name.

items.body: Oxford has certain ghosts to answer for. The Thames Valley once produced a generation of guitar bands who treated distortion less as decoration than physical substance, something capable of swallowing melody and returning it in stranger shapes. Violet Oscillation comes from that same ground, and on their debut EP, it has become clear to me that all those who seek sounds deeply aware of the inheritance without behaving like a museum exhibit dedicated to 1991. Across five densely layered songs, guitars buckle, blur, bend sideways, then dissolve into banks of reverb where the human voice becomes another instrument caught inside the machinery. Veil establishes the method with glide guitar bent into great slabs of pitch and pressure. The My Bloody Valentine connection is obvious, yet Violet Oscillation understands that imitation begins where curiosity ends. Their guitars keep shifting underfoot, with chords smeared across one another until melody appears almost accidentally through the distortion. The track has tremendous weight, though its movement remains oddly weightless, as if the amplifier stacks had somehow learned to levitate. All Meaning Was Whole pushes further into that overloaded guitar language. Layers accumulate until individual parts become difficult to isolate, which is precisely where the song becomes interesting. There are melodies buried everywhere, rising briefly from the mass before being folded back into it. The performance has the strange emotional scale that made shoegaze compelling in the first place: private feeling blown up to architectural dimensions, bedroom uncertainty projected across a wall of amplifiers. Primordial Learning, featuring Abstract in Sound, shifts toward the airier end of Violet Oscillation’s vocabulary. Slowdive and Cocteau Twins hover somewhere in the ancestry, particularly in the suspended vocals and soft-focus guitar treatments, while the arrangement maintains a restless interior motion. Voices drift through overlapping effects, guitars hang in elongated chords, and each new layer seems to widen the room by another impossible few feet. Ethereal, featuring Abstract in Sound, maintains Slowdive’s gauzy style with a slow-moving layer of dreamy haze that resonates with an otherworldly, euphoric energy. It flutters, with stereo channels moving apart and together, creating a calming yet disorienting effect, reminiscent of floating upward and descending toward murmuring angels, or entering a parallel universe. The song smoothly shifts to a gentle marching drum beat as it fades away. Visual Snow closes the EP in a thick blur of texture, melody, and accumulated noise. The title fits: everything seems visible yet unstable, as though the music were being perceived through an electrical haze. Lovesliescrushing provides another useful reference point here, especially in the manner that guitar becomes atmosphere, mass, and motion simultaneously. Violet Oscillation have spent years embedded in shoegaze culture through Pedal Partners, signature effects pedals, and connections extending from Kevin Shields’ Fender Blender launch to Slowdive’s Simon Scott. None of that biography would mean much if these songs could not carry themselves. Fortunately, they can. it has become clear to me that all those who seek finds Violet Oscillation treating shoegaze as a living vocabulary: guitars bent beyond polite recognition, voices suspended inside great clouds of amplification, and four songs determined to discover how much feeling can be packed into distortion before the speakers finally surrender. items.body: On A Violent Power and Bontempi Pop 3, Danz CM treats synthesizers less like collector’s trophies than working machinery, using vintage hardware to build pop that moves, mutates, and occasionally grins at its own oscillations. The equipment may be old, but the decisions feel immediate: basslines snap into position, keyboards dart through the margins, and every unusual texture seems enlisted because it can push the song somewhere useful. A Violent Power is the straighter shot. Constructed entirely from analogue synths, it runs on a rigid new-wave pulse that suggests Kraftwerk’s immaculate engineering after somebody slipped a little danger into the control room. Berlin and Ladytron provide useful coordinates, particularly in the marriage of cool surfaces and emotional excess, yet Danz gives the track enough pressure to keep the references from swallowing it. The song concerns surrendering to an overpowering emotion, and the arrangement keeps tightening around that idea, adding momentum until submission starts sounding suspiciously pleasurable. Synth lines rise, retreat, and lock together with the tidy aggression of machinery designed for dancing. Then Bontempi Pop 3 wanders into stranger territory and steals the double single. Its breakbeat shuffles with trip-hop weight while an Italian Bontempi toy organ squeaks, chirps, and zips across the track as though somebody left a children’s keyboard unsupervised in an experimental studio. Broadcast supplies some of its crooked sweetness, while the toy-box melodies carry the idyllic whimsy of Danish synth band Moral, and the repetition has Stereolab’s playful momentum. Just this side of psychedelia, the arrangement keeps producing small surprises without turning into a crowded demonstration of gear. The subject is time: specifically, the desire to escape its disappearing act by occupying the present more completely. That could easily become heavy-handed philosophy, but Danz wisely gives the idea movement rather than solemnity. The beat keeps walking forward while those peculiar keyboards seem determined to distract the clock. Together, the singles reveal a musician with enough technical command to know that technical command is boring when displayed for its own sake. Live guitars, acoustic drums, motorik rhythms, layered vocals, and banks of synthesizers enter according to function rather than prestige, allowing touches of Nation of Language, Chromatics, Ladytron, Stereolab, and Broadcast to flash past without turning the songs into record-collection bookkeeping. A Violent Power provides the immediate hook, but Bontempi Pop 3 supplies the mischief. One is streamlined and commanding; the other keeps poking holes in its own geometry. Listen to A Violent Power/Bontempi Pop 3 below or via the streaming service of your choice here: Originally from New York’s Catskill Mountains and now based in Los Angeles, Danz CM first built an audience during the 2010s as Computer Magic, operating with a staunch DIY approach that eventually produced records including 2015’s Davos and led to considerable success in Japan, where her music appeared in campaigns for Panasonic and Kewpie Mayo. After retiring the Computer Magic name, she moved further into composition and instrumental arrangement, scoring independent films including While Mortals Sleep and Gary Hustwit’s The Map. During the pandemic she also founded Synth History, the print publication devoted to synthesizers, electronic music, and the people behind them, while continuing to write, produce, mix, art-direct, and release music through her own Channel 9 Records. Recent releases have moved from the ambient abstractions of MYTHS to the krautrock excursions of 2025’s LÄRM!, alongside tours supporting LCD Soundsystem and Ladytron. items.album: Death Drifts Under the Skin in Traitrs’ Video for “I Was Ill, You Were Wrong”
items.artist: “As We Dance With Tears in The Rain”
items.excerpt: And I see your sadness Is it just like mine? We spend much of life rehearsing permanence. items.body: And I see your sadness Is it just like mine? We spend much of life rehearsing permanence. Calendars extend months ahead, plans multiply, and ordinary chores encourage the soothing fiction that tomorrow is already ours. Mortality remains manageable as long as it stays abstract, assigned to strangers or some distant version of ourselves. Grief breaks that arrangement. One absence can make every future date feel provisional, exposing distraction as one of the mind’s most useful shelters. “As We Dance With Tears in The Rain” — Death Drifts Under the Skin in Traitrs Video for “I Was Ill, You Were Wrong” That shelter is nearly universal. Work, desire, entertainment, ambition, and the small obligations of the day let us function while the knowledge of an ending waits at the edge of thought. When that knowledge presses forward, it carries a second fear with it: the possibility of losing every person, object, memory, and role through which we understand ourselves. Continuing to move after facing that fact can become its own form of courage. Toronto coldwave act TRAITRS confronts that contradiction in the new video for “I Was Ill, You Were Wrong,” released last November and later included on the band’s album POSSESSOR; the song begins with private anguish before reaching toward the possibility that another person’s grief may resemble our own. “I Was Ill, You Were Wrong is challenging The Psychology of Ignoring Death.” The recording begins beneath low, echoing synths, its measured dirge already gathering force. A disciplined drumbeat dances in the face of death, pulling the song forward as the guitars climb through serrated sweeps, widening melodies, and mounting sheets of effects. Shawn Tucker’s voice carries the cracked theatricality associated with Robert Smith and Brett Anderson while retaining its own bruised register, rising from a controlled ache toward the sound of a heart crying out against erasure. Each confession lands like a brick dropped onto a bare floor. The verses catalogue bodily harm through blunt images of starvation, wires, poison, and a fatal fall; the chorus turns outward, searching another person’s face for the same sorrow. There is a curious reversal within the arrangement: as the dirge-like synths grow heavier, the song seems to quicken, converting dread into momentum. Midway through, an organ-like phrase drives the track into a broader ascent before cascading vocals and guitars accumulate into a dense wall of sound, carrying the music to its greatest height precisely where the subject closes in on extinction. When the single first appeared, Tucker described the shared recognition at its center: “I felt that song connected me to everything and everyone, it is the one thing we all share and have in common,” Tucker said. “It is also a wake up call to live the life you want to live. We only have one chance at this so go dance in the rain.” Directed by Tucker and filmed in severe black and white, the video places Emmanuelle Vaughan inside a space without visible walls, floor, or horizon. She first appears at a distance beneath a narrow overhead light, nearly motionless, before the camera moves close to her collarbone, spine, hands, and face. An oil-dark coating begins to spread across her fingers, arms, back, and throat as her gestures become more expansive. Between these passages, Tucker performs at the microphone and guitar through smoke, coarse grain, and bands of video interference. Vaughan keeps dancing while her body is gradually claimed by the surrounding black, until the final movements yield to an empty frame. Tucker explains: “I find myself personally active in ignoring mortality. It’s inescapable and we use distraction as defence against it. We all crave purpose and everyday distractions. This is a psychological defense mechanism keeping our deepest fears at bay. Our fight for survival. Death has a way of playing with us, bringing up this deep sense of isolation and failure that we are all constantly running away from. Most people find the concept of being completely alone terrifying and painful. It’s stealing our tomorrows, it steals away everything. This album is incredibly personal for me because I’m still trying to make sense of a major loss in my own life. When I directed this, the goal was to visualize death as this unstoppable force—almost like a terminal illness creeping through the body. It doesn’t care who you are; it just destroys. But I didn’t want the video to just be bleak. It’s about our internal fight. I had wrapped the ‘Burn In Heaven’ video up a few months prior and was thinking about casting for I Was Ill and wanted to work with Emma again on this project as the lead and push her in a completely different approach. I also knew Emma knows exactly what I was looking for, and expected of her. In the video, she is aware death has come, but she still chooses to dance, finding this beautiful defiance right up until the black void completely takes over. It was all shot in one day on location in a small studio warehouse in Hamilton, Ontario, that took 7 hours.” The visual idea draws from Jonathan Glazer’s Under the Skin, particularly its limitless black chamber, where space loses every familiar coordinate and solitude becomes physical. Here, the setting turns mortality into an encroaching presence that can be seen on the body. Vaughan understands what has entered the room, yet her dance continues for as long as movement remains possible. “The void represented Ultimate Isolation perfectly and supports my visual theme of total isolation. There are no walls, no horizons, and no exit. The victims are entirely alone with their desires right before they are destroyed.” Tucker reduces the premise to one plain sentence: “None of us are getting out of here alive.” Within the song and video, that certainty becomes a reason to recognize another person’s sadness, inhabit the present, and dance while the body still answers. Watch the video for “I Was Ill, You Were Wrong” below: Formed in Toronto in 2015, TRAITRS began as a recording project before sessions with producer Josh Korody led to the 2016 debut Rites and Ritual. Butcher’s Coin followed in 2018, expanding the band’s audience across North America and Europe, while 2021’s Horses in the Abattoir brought another set of propulsive rhythms, angular guitars, and horror-informed electronics. Years of touring have carried TRAITRS through more than a dozen countries, including appearances at Wave-Gotik-Treffen, Castle Party, and Canadian Music Week, as well as shows with VNV Nation, Lebanon Hanover, She Past Away, Twin Tribes, and Ultra Sunn. POSSESSOR, released March 13, 2026, brings the band’s preoccupation with grief, alienation, and mortality into its most personal form to date. Recorded at Toronto’s Wychwood Studios with Josh Korody and mastered by Matt Colton, the album is available to stream here and order through Bandcamp here. items.body: I need to know And maybe we can talk about And maybe we can try to solve it Take me by the hand and take me away Heartbreak rarely proceeds with literary dignity. People sulk, contradict themselves, make declarations they abandon ten minutes later, and discover that wounded pride is a lousy substitute for company. The same voice that insists, “I don’t need you,” can soon confess, “I miss you.” French Police build their new double single, Super Over Drive / Silver, around that reversal, tracing the distance between defensive solitude and the admission that another person is still wanted. The release follows July’s Reptile / Japan, the double single that opened the Chicago trio’s new chapter with Interscope Records. On Reptile, Brian Flores looked toward companionship as a possible escape from thoughts he could not quiet. Super Over Drive takes that need into more combative territory, allowing loneliness to sour into anger before Silver strips away the posture and asks whether speaking plainly might still save something. French Police have spent the better part of their existence making romantic catastrophe sound unusually well-dressed, and these paired songs carry that instinct into bigger, cleaner arrangements without disguising the embarrassment in the words. There is still enough black-clad cool here to populate three basement clubs, but Flores sounds increasingly willing to let the mask slip, giving both songs their peculiar charge. Super Over Drive runs on a bass line with the stubborn forward motion of somebody walking home at 3 a.m. because calling a cab would require admitting the night went badly. The rhythm section keeps everything locked down while Manny Herrera’s guitar rises, retreats, then slices back through the arrangement from another angle. Flores stretches his phrasing farther than usual, holding notes until the romantic detachment begins to crack. His voice carries composure and panic simultaneously, a useful combination for a song about insisting you can live without anybody while secretly hoping somebody will notice you are drowning in your own apartment. Directed by Chris Eichenseer, the accompanying video frames the band through a sepia-tinted, abstract performance that feels appropriately unstable. Bodies blur into movement, faces appear and disappear through unusual compositions, and the muted brown tones give the footage the quality of some damaged transmission dug out of an abandoned television studio. It is moody, slightly trippy, and strange in exactly the right proportions, extending the song’s sense of emotional dislocation without explaining any of it away. Watch the video for Super Over Drive below: Silver turns the temperature down, balancing spacious guitar interplay, vocal reach, and carefully controlled escalation while leaving more room around Flores’ voice. Here the problem is communication itself: caring without saying so, sensing that something has broken, and wondering whether two people can still name the damage before it becomes permanent. The song carries guilt without theatrical punishment. Its final admissions of absence and need land with the blunt force of somebody finally saying what should have been said weeks earlier. Watch the video for Silver below: Founded by Mexican-American singer, songwriter, and guitarist Brian Flores in 2018, French Police—with Herrera on lead guitar and Rolando Donjuan on bass—came out of Chicago with obvious debts to Interpol while steadily developing a romantic severity closer to the international post-punk culture surrounding Molchat Doma, Lebanon Hanover, The Chameleons, and KINO. At the very moment a major-label deal promises to enlarge their world, Super Over Drive and Silver keep French Police focused on the smaller disaster: two people sitting close enough to speak, each waiting for the other to go first. items.body: There are places that become so closely associated with geopolitics that it is easy to forget they are still inhabited landscapes, with their own geology, ecosystems and daily rhythms. Qeshm Island, in the Strait of Hormuz, Iran, is one such place. On Aerial Roots, Mo Farzaneh turns his attention to the island itself, drawing on field recordings made across its coastlines, villages, mountains and Hara mangrove forests. Wind, birds, water and traces of human activity are woven into electronics that grow directly from the environments he encountered. As Farzaneh explains in our interview, repeated visits taught him to recognise structures already present in the soundscape: changes in density across day and night, shifting winds and, above all, the tides, whose cycles repeat without ever producing exactly the same configuration. “Tabl” opens with wind carrying faint evidence of human presence through crackling environmental noise and birdsong, while sweeping shifts in pitch from a rising and falling wail give the piece a ghostly atmosphere. “Doulab” becomes more languid, bringing water and birds into sharper focus as an incantatory, revolving figure recalls the doulab, the traditional water wheel from which the piece takes its name. Circularity becomes still more pronounced on “Distant Memories”, where the movement of waves is translated into electronic material. Farzaneh describes the sea as an image of memory: each wave replaces the previous one while the underlying rhythm persists. The thirteen-minute “Aerial Roots” pushes this exchange further, playing with resonance until the natural ecosystem begins to resemble a negative imprint of its synthesised counterpart; towards the end, the environmental sounds gradually reclaim the foreground. “Sandstone Canyon”, meanwhile, introduces sharper sonic peaks and greater dynamic variation. The title catches something essential about Farzaneh’s method. Roots normally imply attachment to a particular ground; these roots have become airborne. His field recordings retain evidence of actual places and events, while percussive elements carry traces of particular practices, yet both can be detached, transformed and recomposed. Farzaneh noticed how Qeshm’s acoustic environment changes near piers and other centres of human activity, where species audible in quieter areas disappear beneath the noise of boats, while human sounds themselves can become strangely disembodied. Having moved to Qeshm after years in Tehran, he approaches the island as a stranger learning how to listen, deliberately resisting the temptation to interpret the lives he encounters. The album never turns these concerns into an environmental manifesto. Instead, vulnerability is embedded in its shifting cycles, where repetition always contains small changes and nothing remains sonically fixed. As Farzaneh writes of the Hara mangroves, this is “an ecosystem whose cycles have repeated here for thousands of years, now seeming more fragile than ever.” photo by Mo Farzaneh To find out more about the location and the recording process we asked Mo Farzaneh a few questions. Aerial Roots grew out of recordings made across Qeshm Island, from the Hara mangrove forests and coastline to mountains and villages, and you describe field recording less as collecting material than as a way of “spending time with a place”. Listening to the album, birds, water, wind and other environmental sounds often seem to determine the music’s rhythm and structure rather than simply provide atmosphere. How much did the environments themselves teach you how to compose? Were there moments when you found yourself following patterns already present in water, birdsong or wind rather than imposing a musical structure upon them? Yes, a lot. At the beginning of my field recording work, it was mostly the sound events themselves that caught my attention. But gradually I stopped thinking only about collecting raw material. I kept going back to the same places at different times, and I started noticing how the sound environment changed with the weather or with human activity. Those repeated visits made the place itself show me its rhythms and patterns. The way the density of sound shifted throughout the day and night was already a kind of musical structure. I just listened to it and tried to keep that structure in the composition. The electronic parts are basically my emotional and inner response to those patterns more like a conversation between the sounds of the place and my own reaction as someone who was there listening. I should also say that after years of living in Tehran, moving to Qeshm felt completely different. The unfamiliarity of that listening environment changed the way I hear things, and that shift still feels valuable to me. photo by Mo Farzaneh Your photographs repeatedly move between very large landscapes and extremely close observations of surfaces: eroded rock, cracked earth, tidal patterns in sand, mangrove roots, weathered walls. There is something similar in the music, where a recognisable environment can suddenly seem to dissolve into microscopic textures, drones and electronic detail. When you were photographing, recording and composing on Qeshm, did these different ways of looking and listening begin to influence one another? And do you see the photographs as documentation of the places behind Aerial Roots, or as another part of the same artistic work? Yes, I had already started photographing on the island before I began recording sound. Looking through the camera helped the direction of the project become clearer. Gradually I noticed that photography was affecting the sound sources I chose, and the other way around working on the sounds pushed me to take more photos, and more varied ones. Sometimes looking at a place through the camera while listening to it at the same time also changed how I structured the pieces or processed the sounds. Making this album and connecting with the place through these different ways made me want to share the other things I had collected too. That’s why I see the photographs as part of the work itself, not just documentation. They’re both telling the same experience, just from different angles. photo by Mo Farzaneh In your notes on the Hara mangroves, you describe an extraordinarily organised daily sound cycle: birds and other creatures gradually becoming more active, frogs joining the soundscape, crickets occupying the night, and the first bird at dawn effectively marking another transition. You also describe the ecosystem as having repeated these cycles for thousands of years while now appearing “more fragile than ever”. There is a comparable tension in Aerial Roots between repetition and constant small change. Did those ecological cycles provide a model for the album’s sense of musical time, and how consciously did the environmental vulnerability of Qeshm enter the work? Yes, but it was more a matter of gradually becoming aware of it. Because I was recording in the forest at different times of day and night, I started paying closer attention to how the environment was changing. I slowly noticed a recurring cycle things would repeat, but they were always slightly different. Even now, whenever I go back to those recordings, I hear something new. The changes weren’t just about day and night. The tides played a big role too. The activity of the creatures in the forest seemed to move with the tide, constantly shifting the sound. Places that at first seemed completely still were actually changing all the time. The wind direction could change several times in a day, the light would move across the water, and a bird I heard from one direction in the morning might come from somewhere else in the afternoon. Even something as repetitive as the daily cycle of the forest took on a slightly different shape each time. This gave me a strong sense of the tension between stability and constant small change a pattern that repeats without ever being exactly the same. That quality became something I paid attention to while working on the album. I tried to keep a similar feeling in the structure of the pieces. I was also constantly aware of how vulnerable Qeshm’s natural environment is in the face of human presence. The more I moved around the island, the clearer this became. Many of the quieter places, simply because they were further from busier areas, had a completely different sonic character. There were bird sounds you simply don’t hear near the piers, where the noise and activity of boats made the environment very different. That contrast stayed with me throughout the process. photo by Mo Farzaneh Memory seems to occupy an important place in Aerial Roots, most explicitly in the title “Distant Memories.” Field recording might initially appear to be an act of preservation — fixing a particular place and moment in time — yet your electronic processing allows those recordings to move away from their original form and acquire new associations. How do you understand the relationship between remembering and transforming in your work? Are you interested in preserving something of Qeshm as you experienced it, or in allowing those memories to change and acquire a new life through composition? Being part of this process made me think more about my relationship with places. No recording can fully represent a place. It can only capture one layer of the experience of being there tied to that specific day and time. What remains is a kind of sonic memory, and that memory keeps changing. When I enter an unfamiliar place, I usually slow down and listen before trying to understand what I’m hearing. Sound leaves more room for imagination than a fixed visual image. I start to experience the space less as something solid and more as something alive and constantly shifting. Listening to something unstable and fleeting feels closely connected to memory for me. A sound happens, disappears, and becomes part of what I remember. When I return to it later, I’m not necessarily hearing the same thing anymore. The recording is still there, but my relationship to it has changed. This became especially clear while working on “Distant Memories.” I took the continuous sound of the sea and worked with it in a way that keeps the underlying rhythm of the waves, but never lets any single wave stay for long. As one wave arrives, it gradually replaces the previous one, and then it too fades as the next one takes its place. In a way, the piece became an image of how memory works for me: something arrives, stays for a moment, and is slowly replaced. We don’t necessarily lose the memory completely, but its original form becomes more distant each time. The sea felt like a continuous memory the rhythm remains, but the individual waves are always temporary. That’s probably what interested me about it in the first place. photo by Mo Farzaneh Qeshm is not only an extraordinary natural environment but an island with a remarkably layered human history: inhabited since prehistoric times, shaped by successive empires and occupations, and for centuries positioned along maritime routes connecting Iran with India, China and East Africa. Your notes, however, approach the island at a much more intimate scale — people talking between houses, fishermen working on their nets, a goatherd calling in the morning, children cycling through a village, or someone inviting you into their home and offering you dates. What is your own personal relationship with Qeshm, and how much did you want Aerial Roots to engage not only with its landscapes and ecosystems but with the lives, histories and cultural memory of the people who inhabit them? My personal relationship with Qeshm is that of a stranger who’s gradually getting to know a place. Maybe that distance is why things that feel ordinary and everyday to the people who live there still feel fresh and worth noticing to me. That sense of newness is what made me want to listen to them and record them. As I spent time going around different villages and parts of the island, I started to sense something of the island’s history and collective memory in the rhythms of everyday life, rather than in its buildings or official stories. The way people adapt to the climate and their environment, and the kind of resilience in how they live, really stood out. The closer I listened, the harder it became to draw a clear line between the natural and human soundscapes of the island. For me, people’s lives were just as much a part of Qeshm’s soundscape as the mangroves or the sea. Since I was a stranger myself, still learning how to listen to this place and the people in it, I preferred not to explain or interpret their lives. I just let their presence stay part of my experience of the island. Maybe that’s why what I saw and heard found its way more into the sounds I chose and the overall atmosphere of the album than into talking about it directly. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: It's been a while since we've visited with one of my favorite "microscenes" - the French stoner and doom metal scene. Luckily, one of my favorite bands from that area of the world are back with a new album this year and have graciously afforded me the privilege of premiering a single from said album. I covered Pelegrin for the first time four years ago with another premiere and I've been waiting for more music since then. Happily, "Sun and Blood" does not disappoint with a trippy, occult-steeped video and, more importantly, a more muscular and present approach to Pelegrin's sound than before. Head on down below to take the journey!Pelegrin's previous music can be described as "airy", a certain thinness which worked very well with the expansive can of psychedelia they were going for. But here, the adjective would be "earthy" - the main riff is much more present in the mix, its tone thicker and heavier. The drums are punctual like falling stones, lending the track momentum and groove. Sprinkle in the same excellent vocals from the previous release, one scorching, desert-sun hot solo, and a few more touches here and there from excellent backing riffs and thick bass, and you've got yourself a treat. I also love the lighter guitars which open the track, setting the ground for the shimmering, stoner sound the band is so good for."Sun and Blood" comes to us from the upcoming The Curse of Nephtar, due to release on September 4th on the mighty Ripple Music. You can head on over here to pre-order it (and also check out that glorious art work in full).

items.body: Arguably the defining metal band of their generation, Mastodon have never had a bad album, but their last four outings have been a significant step below the original classic four records that put them on the map. Beginning with the simultaneously simplified yet unfocused and maybe misguided The Hunter in 2011 and ending with the surprisingly successful and deeply personal, yet somehow forgettable double album Hushed and Grim (2021), the second chapter of Mastodon's career has been characterised by paradoxical inconsistencies. Although the band continued to push themselves with new concepts and textures, it also seemed like they'd fallen into something of a reliable holding pattern, emerging every few years to deliver something comfortingly yet never that excitingly Mastodon sounding. Marrow Deep, therefore, represents the beginning of a new chapter for Mastodon,* and presents an opportunity for the band to refresh and re-establish themselves, which they have taken to wholeheartedly. Whatever you think of the albums in between, it's hard to deny that Marrow Deep is the best Mastodon album since Once More 'round the Sun (2014)—or even longer, for (silly) people who don't like that album for whatever reason. The record continuously conjures up the Mastodonian triumphs of their past, with its overall sonic palette and songwriting sensibilities are something of a mix between what are perhaps the band's two greatest triumphs in Blood Mountain (2006) and Crack the Skye (2009). Even then though, it sounds less like a rehash or a missing link than something like what Emperor of Sand (2017) could and maybe should have been, in its masterful blend of classic and continuous Mastodon sounds.There are also a few new elements in play. Along with the added keyboards and emphasis on more traditional prog rock textures, "In the Ruins" represents something of a progressive metal Ouroboros, sounding like the sort of song Baroness have been ending their shows with since 2012, while "A Vampire's Demeanor" (featuring Lamb of God's Randy Blythe and Converge's Nate Newton) is an almost nu metal sounding song that joins Meshuggah's "Monstro-City" as perhaps one of the finest modern examples of the genre. This is also the first time Mastodon are working with Converge's Kurt Ballou and co-producer Patrik Berger, who is mostly known for co-writing Robyn's "Dancing on my Own" and a bunch of Charli XCX songs. Neither producer's trademark sound is really present though, with both combining instead into a perfect balance of metallic crunch and progressive clarity.Marrow Deep is, of course, the first Mastodon album without iconic founding guitarist Brent Hinds, who was ejected from the band last year, amid what appear to be increasingly troubling circumstances, before dying in a motorcycle accident a few months later. Hinds has since been replaced by Canadian guitarist Nick Johnston, whose work I am not familiar with, but who seems to be a good fit. In fact, Johnston does such a good job of fitting in that it's hard to really tell if he's there at all—whether he does such a good job of blending in with the rest of the band, or if he wasn't really that involved in the album's composition and is simply playing parts written with Hinds in mind. Conversely, Hinds' absence, while not necessarily damaging, is certainly noticeable. There are plenty of killer leads across the record, but none of them rip or ripple with the kind of fire he brought to the table. While he was certainly the least-accomplished of the three Mastodon vocalists, the absence of Hinds' distinctively garbled voice somewhat diminishes the album's dynamics, with Troy Sanders solidifying himself as the band's dedicated vocalist and Brann Dailor only really brought in as an added flavour here or there. You can hear the parts where Hinds' might have come in, and it makes you wonder what Marrow Deep might have been if he had continued on with the band instead.During this shake-up, Mastodon also took the opportunity to officially induct into their ranks Brazilian keyboardist João Nogueira, who has been collaborating with the band since 2021 and also plays in The Claypool Lennon Delirium. Unlike Johnston, Nogueira's contributions are immediately noticeable and largely elevating. Rather than dominating the album's atmosphere, his key sections are more often brought in as little flourishes during bridge and lead sections, that add such an exciting and distinctly "progressive" air to proceedings that it's a wonder Mastodon didn't introduce him or another keyboardist sooner. Unfortunately, while he might be a perfect sonic fit for the band, his personal associations raise some serious concerns. Outside of music, Nogueira has a longstanding association with conservative/right-wing, historical "revisionist" organisation Brasil Paralelo, where he goes by the name "Rasta" and hosts a sort of Daily Show-style comedy show. I don't speak Portuguese, so I can't comment on what he's actually saying in these videos, but—given Brasil Paralelo's associations with the rise of modern, neo-facisim, and their documented defenses and conspiracy theories about things like colonialism, slavery, sexism, homophobia and more—it's probably not good and certainly isn't being published somewhere that is. Hinds certainly had his own problems, but there's a big difference between personal gripes and uncoothness and being a mouthpiece for an institutionalised and (somewhat) influential right-wing conspiracy-spreading organisation. As far as I know, Mastodon have not addressed Nogueira's involvement with Brasil Paralelo in any interviews or other press material, and it is unclear whether they are aware of, or aware of the extent to which he serves as a spreader of their harmful, right-wing rhetoric, but I—and I'm sure many other Mastodon fans—are very interested to see how they respond once it is brought up.Additionally, for all its brilliant excesses, there's one other thing clearly missing from Marrow Deep, and that's big, fat, fuck-off riffs. The band's trademark, wiry guitar leads are on full display, and there are plenty of killer moments to be had throughout the songs—often simultaneously—but there's no "March of the Fire Ants", "Blood and Thunder", "High Road" or "Curl of the Burl" here, and hardly a "Wolf is Loose", "Oblivion", "Teardrinker" or "Sultan's Curse" either. Lead single "Your Ghost Again" is clearly the album's standout song, though that has far more to do with its luscious progressive layering and vocal melodies than the force of its six-string savagery. Opener "Barbarians Blood" lumbers rather than roars in, and while "Out like a Lamb" perhaps comes closest to becoming a classic Mastodon rocker, it's more in the "Spectrelight" style of anachronistic throwbacks than its own, definitive statement. Maybe its the lack of Hinds' contributions to its composition, but—as good as they all are—none of Marrow Deep's tracks announce themselves in the way the true Mastodon classics do.The other, arguably minor—but also rather unnecessary—weakness of Marrow Deep is its length. Mastodon have never been ones for short record lengths, with most of their outings sitting around the 50-minute mark. Considering the complexity of their compositions though, this length usually makes for a surprising and rewardingly concise experience, especially when it comes to something like Crack the Skye. At 65 minutes, Marrow Deep is easily Mastodon's longest, single-disc experience and you definitely feel it. What's more, the responsibility for this arguably bloated longevity lies squarely on superfluous final outing "The Three Fates." The album already had something of a false/elongated ending with "A Vampire's Demeanor," which provided a perfectly natural climax, before "The Vanishing" comes slinking in for one more round. Here, the encore presentation works perfectly, with the very "Planet Caravan"-sounding track —which features the actual Black Sabbath's Geezer Butler, alongside Gojira's Joe Duplantier—adding a natural and fitting epilogue to proceedings, whose spaced-out sounds allow the listener time to "come down" and reflect on the journey they've just been on—only to have "Three Fates" come crashing in again and ruin the whole effect, only to awkwardly end on a random riff that comes out of nowhere and simply stops suddenly. The song itself isn't bad and worth it on its own just to hear Clutch's Neil Fallon carrying on like a mad preacher, but I'd definitely say its the weakest track on here though and not nearly as suitable for closing the record as the two tracks before it, and might have worked better earlier on in the album.** As is, however, it feels tacked on and an instance of over-egging the progressive pudding.Marrow Deep is an album that asks a lot of its listeners, as the last couple Mastodon albums have as well. Unlike its immediate predecessors though, Marrow Deep feels fresh and inspired, pushing forward once again when it felt like Mastodon had maybe run out of things to say. While it sounds distinctly like Mastodon, it also sounds like a band who are still hungry and aren't satisfied to rest on their laurels the way they arguably have been for a while now. Get a few more riffs in there, cut down on the length and sort out the whole keyboardist situation, and they might yet be capable of delivering another definitive classic. Marrow Deep by Mastodon *Take a shot every time someone writes that while reviewing this album.**Due to promo streaming's penchant for playing final tracks second when listening on mobile for some reason, I can confirm it does indeed work quite well as the second rather than final track.

items.body: Thierry Kiranga was born in Katana, in the Democratic Republic of Congo, on the shores of Lake Kivu, and raised across the border in Bujumbura, Burundi, before civil war forced him to Italy. His new single, “Hard Times,” follows March’s “Ciao” and arrived July 17 on Roble Records. He learned to sing and to play guitar, drums and percussion under two Burundian mentors, Jean Christophe Matata and Canjo Amissi. Music ran in the family before that: his mother founded and still directs the Santa Cecilia choir, and his father sang tenor with the SOSAT choir and played violin on some of Italy’s earliest television broadcasts. Kiranga later studied Afro-Cuban jazz at Milan’s CPM conservatory, specialising in drums and percussion, and released his debut album, Asante, in the summer of 2023. “Hard Times” was recorded at Roble Factory Studio in Alghero, Sardinia, produced and mixed by Antonio Leardi and mastered by Simone Squillario. Choral harmonies sit over rhythms drawn from Kiranga’s Afro-Caribbean and European influences.The lyrics call out a broken promise: a world that claims to offer safety and prosperity while treating anyone different as a threat. Kiranga’s answer is to look to older generations for guidance, the same instinct that sent him to Matata and Amissi as a teenager and that he grew up watching in his own parents. On stage, Kiranga performs with an eight-piece band, The Backyard Embassy, drawing bass, guitar, keys, percussion, horns and backing vocals from players based across Italy, France, the US and Bulgaria. Stream “Hard Times” HERE The post Daily Discovery: Thierry – Hard Times appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: 2026.08.28 「建築家が聴いた音楽―建築家・土浦亀城の思考に響いた音」演奏会シリーズ 第3回「内面としてのロマン派：シューベルト」 建築家・土屋亀城（1897–1996）がどのような音楽を、どのような感覚で聴いていたのか。「建築家が聴いた音楽―建築家・土浦亀城の思考に響いた音」は、昭和初期の住宅建築を代表する名作・土浦亀城邸で、音楽作品を演奏し、対話によって思考を深める、全6回の対話型演奏会シリーズ。 9月16日（水）にひらかれるシリーズ第3回は、「内面としてのロマン派：シューベルト」。今ここでシューベルトを聴く企図を、本演奏会シリーズで総合監修・ナビゲーターを務める、音楽学者の久保田慶一先生に伺いました。 ONTOMO編集部 東京・神楽坂にある音楽之友社を拠点に、Webマガジン「ONTOMO」の企画・取材・編集をしています。「音楽っていいなぁ、を毎日に。」を掲げ、やさしく・ふかく・おもしろ... 詳しく見る 建築と音楽を対話で紐解く深い体験 ——「建築家が聴いた音楽―建築家・土浦亀城の思考に響いた音」はどのような演奏会シリーズでしょうか。 久保田 今回の演奏会シリーズのコンセプトは、建築と音楽の接点として、6つの視点から音楽を聴くことにあります。構造、くつろぎ、内面、色彩、均整、素材という視点です。 建築には構造が必要ですが、音楽には楽器、音階、音楽のそれぞれの構造があります。自宅で人々はくつろぎ、音楽を聴いてもくつろぎます。また物思いにふけって自分の内面を見つめるには、静かな空間が必要です。内装の色、全体の均整、素材がそこに住むわれわれの感性を刺激し、また同時に、やすらぎを与えます。 建築と音楽のそれぞれが作る空間を楽しむことが、今回のシリーズの目的です。建物のなかに入って「ここに住んでみたい」、「ここで音楽を聴いてみたい」という願いを叶えてくれる演奏会です。 ©土浦亀城アーカイブズ 土浦亀城邸 東京都指定有形文化財（建造物） 建築家・土浦亀城が米国でフランク・ロイド・ライトに学び、帰国後1935年に竣工した自邸。昭和10年代にあって、現代にも通じるような「健康的な楽しい暮らし」をアイデアで実現し、プライバシーのある空間も備えつつ、文化的な仲間との豊かな時間の共有も叶えた。自然光に満ちた、日本のモダニズム木造住宅を代表する名作。また土浦亀城は、バッハから20世紀音楽に至る幅広いジャンルを好み、電蓄で音楽を聴くことがこの住宅で過ごす愉しみのひとつだった。工夫にあふれた建築は見どころが多く、今回のシューベルト・プログラムと相高めあう空間に演奏会への期待が高まる。 【所在地】東京都港区南青山2-5-13 【原設計】土浦亀城・土浦信子 （1935年 品川区上大崎） 【復原・移築設計】 安田アトリエ 【実測調査・実測図面・模型制作】 東京工業大学安田幸一研究室（当時） ——シリーズ第3回「内面としてのロマン派：シューベルト」では、歌曲にも言葉があり、対話にも言葉が生まれますね。言葉の存在、人間の声が持つ魔法をダイレクトに感じられるのではないかと興味深いです。プログラムの意図や聴きどころをお聞かせください。 久保田 今回演奏される歌曲の歌詞はすべてドイツ語です。プログラムには原語の詩は掲載せずに、日本語訳だけにしてあります。 お話のなかで私が強調したいのは、声を楽器の音として聴いてくださいということです。意味を理解する必要はありません。ドイツ語の子音や母音の連続がつくる響きやリズムを、ラップを聴くように楽しんでもらえればいいと思います。ただしキーワードになる言葉の原語はお伝えして、いっしょに発音してもらうつもりです。例えば、小川を意味する「バッハBach」など。 また私のお話では、詩の内容に関連して、聴衆の方々に、ご自身の経験や記憶を辿っていただきます。今回は恋愛に関する歌曲が多いので、若い日のあるいは現在進行中の恋愛、あるいはそこまでいかなくても、子どもや孫への愛情などについて、私から質問をして、ご自身の内面を掘り下げていただきます。そのうえで、歌曲を聴くことで、その経験や記憶と音楽が「化学変化」を起こします。つまり、音楽を「わたくし事」として聴いてもらうのです。こうすることで、音楽を聴くという経験がより深くなっていきます。 例えば、東日本大震災の復興支援歌として知られた「花は咲く」がありますが、その歌を復興支援歌として聴くのと、亡くなられた祖父母の記憶を思いだして聴くのとでは、歌を聴いたときの印象が異なることは想像できますね。「わたくし事」として音楽を聴くということは、そういうことです。音楽はいかようにも聴いていいわけですね。 久保田慶一（音楽学者） 東京藝術大学大学院修士課程修了。音楽学博士（東京藝術大学大学院）。フライブルク大学、ハンブルク大学、ベルリン自由大学に留学。東京学芸大学教授、国立音楽大学教授・副学長、東京経済大学客員教授を経て、現在、日本大学大学院ならびに放送大学講師。専門は18世紀ドイツ音楽史。『バッハ』（音楽之友社、2021年）他、著書多数。「建築家が聴いた音楽―建築家・土浦亀城の思考に響いた音」では総合監修・ナビゲーターを務める。 ——今回演奏されるテノールの片野耕喜さん、フォルテピアノの小川加恵さんについて教えてください。 久保田 おふたりとも、私とは旧知であり教え子でもあります。彼らの演奏も何度も聴いています。 対話型演奏会を銘打ってはいますが、私と聴衆の方との会話はかなり限られています。そこで、演奏の合間に、私と演奏者が演奏する曲や楽器など、いろんな対話をします。これまで2回演奏会をしましたが、なかなか好評だったようです。 片野耕喜 （テノール） 小川加恵（フォルテピアノ） ——小川さんは貴重なフォルテピアノを演奏されるので、片野さんと小川さんと楽器が土浦亀城邸でどのように響くのか、楽しみです。シューベルトとフォルテピアノの時代・土浦亀城邸の時代をめぐる、時空を超えた体験となりそうですね。楽器の魅力についてもお聞かせください。 久保田 シューベルトは生前、同時代に同じ場所に住んでいたベートーヴェンとは異なり、大きな公的な会場で自作品を演奏したことがありません。「シューベルティアーデ」と呼ばれたサロンで演奏していました。フォルテピアノはそのような空間にぴったりの楽器です。シューベルトの音楽を理解するためには、当時響いた音や空間を経験することが欠くことはできないでしょう。 フォルテピアノ ルイ・ドゥルケンモデル（1790年頃） クリス・マーネ製作（1989年） 音域：FF~f3 （５オクターブ） ダンパー：膝ペダル モデレーター：手動式 message from 小川加恵 今回使用するのは、シューベルトが生まれた頃と同時代、1790年頃のウィーンのフォルテピアノをモデルとした楽器です。現代のピアノとは異なる、軽やかで透明感のある響きと、まるで言葉を語るような繊細な表情が魅力です。   今回はシューベルトの《君がここにいたことを》《ガニュメート》《鱒》、シューマンの《詩人の恋》より《君の目に見入ると》など、詩と音楽が深く結びついた歌曲をお楽しみいただきます。歌詞に描かれた情景や心の機微を、フォルテピアノがどのように「歌い、語る」のかにも耳を傾けていただければと思います。   先見性を持ちながらも、人の暮らしに寄り添う親密な空間として設計された土浦邸と、もともとサロンや家庭など身近な空間で楽しまれていたフォルテピアノ。その親和性から生まれる響きとともに、音楽を間近に感じていただける特別なひとときを私自身とても楽しみにしています。 ——ご来場のみなさまに、本演奏会をたのしむコツやメッセージをお願いします。 久保田 音楽の聴き方は人さまざまです。またこの曲にはこのような聴き方が「ベスト」であるということもありません。一般的な聴き方や傾向はあると思います。 演奏会では、演奏者が身体を通して発した音や音楽を聴き、そこから得られるイメージ、感情、情景を楽しんでもらえればといいと思います。「聴いてよかった」「また同じ曲を、同じ作曲家の、同じ演奏家の音楽を聴いてみたい」と思っていただけるのが、企画者としては「ベスト」です。 音楽は一定の空間の中で聴かれることを想定して作曲され、また演奏されます。空間に響く音の振動は、われわれの人間の皮膚をも振動させています。演奏者と聴衆の身体は、空間と音を介して、共鳴しているとも言えます。こうしたことを経験すること、またその良さを伝えていくことが、今後、音楽が多くの人に愛されていくためには必要であると思っています。
